TASK. You are given the weights of a language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B (text part: 24 layers of width 1,024; layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and 23 are full-attention layers with 8 query heads and 2 key/value heads of size 256 and a gated output, the other 18 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers with 16 heads of size 128; each layer has a SwiGLU MLP of width 3,584; RMSNorm; vocabulary 248,320; input embedding and output layer tied). Your job is to make it better at writing correct programs by EDITING ITS WEIGHTS DIRECTLY: find out what goes wrong inside the network when it fails at programming problems and repair that with targeted changes.

HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED. After you finish, your edited model and the unedited model are evaluated on held-out code-generation benchmarks (Python functions specified by a description with an example test, or by a signature and docstring) with this fixed protocol: the chat template with thinking enabled (enable_thinking=True: the model reasons between <think> and </think>, then answers); the user message is the problem statement, a blank line and "Write a complete, self-contained Python 3 solution. Put your final code in a single ```python block at the end of your answer."; sampling with temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0 and presence penalty 1.5, and at most 32,768 new tokens for reasoning and answer together. The last ```python block after </think> is extracted; only its imports, definitions and top-level assignments are kept (example calls and asserts the model adds are dropped), and it is run in a sandbox against the problem's hidden unit tests, with a time limit. A sample is correct only if every test passes. The config, tokenizer, chat template and decoding settings are fixed: only weight values can change (same tensor names and shapes; your edits are cast to bfloat16, the model's dtype). You never see these benchmarks.

WHAT COUNTS. We want edits that come from understanding the network: find out what goes wrong when it fails at programming problems, identify the components responsible (specific neurons, heads, directions or circuits) and change them in a way you can justify with evidence. Repairing a specific failure mechanism is in scope. For example, if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, because it never closes or never opens its code block, because it drifts into another language or into prose, because it renames the function it was asked for, or because a systematic pattern makes its code fail to parse, then finding and fixing what drives that counts. Out of scope, and refused by save_edit: the final norm (model.language_model.norm.weight), the input embedding / output layer (model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight, which is tied to the output layer), and any edit that only multiplies a whole tensor by a constant. Also out of scope: global knobs (making the whole output distribution sharper or flatter; raising or lowering particular tokens, such as code fences or end-of-turn, regardless of context); making the model skip its thinking or close it early regardless of the problem; and writing particular problems' solutions or test outputs into the weights (memorization edits). Repairing a specific failure inside the thinking or inside the code is in scope.

WHAT YOU HAVE.
1. A persistent Python kernel (no internet, no GPU): variables survive between your code blocks, like a notebook. The model's files are read-only in /model, practice problems read-only in /practice, and /work is your read-write folder. Available: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, PyTorch (CPU), pandas, sympy, networkx, safetensors, transformers (for the tokenizer). Defined in advance: NAMES (the 320 tensor names of the language model; the checkpoint's vision encoder is not used), load(name) (a float32 torch tensor: your current edit if there is one, else the original), load_original(name), save_edit(name, tensor) (stores the edit as /work/edited/<name>.npy), drop_edit(name), edited(), tok (the model's tokenizer), and run_tests(code, problem_id) (runs a piece of code, such as one the model generated, against that practice problem's tests in a separate sandbox and returns {"status": pass, wrong_answer, runtime_error, timeout, syntax_error or wrong_interface, "exc": the exception type of a runtime error}; this runs the code, not the model). Gradients are disabled. To run code, reply with exactly one block that starts with a line ```python and ends with a line ```; if its last line is an expression, its value is shown. Inside a block, do not start any line with ``` (build such strings with '`' * 3 instead), or the block may be cut there. One execution may take up to 900 seconds and 14 GB of memory; output is cut at 10,000 characters. You may run code up to 300 times. If the kernel is restarted (time or memory limit), its variables are lost and you are told so; files in /work stay.
2. Practice problems with tests (none of them is in the evaluation), one JSON object per line with id, source, split, difficulty, problem (the exact user message the model is given, instruction included), test_format ("function": entry_point, tests as assert statements, test_setup; "stdio": tests as {"input", "output"} pairs, output compared with whitespace normalized) and reference (a solution that passes the tests): /practice/mbpp_practice.jsonl (319 short function-writing problems from the MBPP train, validation and prompt splits; each problem statement shows one of its tests), /practice/apps_practice.jsonl (1,400 APPS train problems whose programs read standard input: 34 introductory, 1,077 interview, 289 competition; at most 10 tests each). Choose whichever serve your experiments.
3. A forward-pass tool with a budget of 20 forward passes in total. A forward pass is one of two things, and each counts as one pass regardless of its size or how long it takes. Every result names its request number <k>, which appears in its file names.
 (a) GENERATION: the model answers up to 512 generations (items x samples) with the evaluation's protocol. Reply with exactly one block that starts with ```forward and contains JSON:
 {"type": "generate", "model": "original", "edited" or "both", "problems": ["<practice id>", ...], "prompts": ["<your own user message>", ...] (optional), "n": samples per item (items x n <= 512; with "both" <= 256 per model), "max_tokens": at most 32768 (the default), "activations": {"layers": [hidden indices 0..24], "mlp": [decoder layers 0..23]} (optional)}
 Instead of a long list you can give "problems_file" or "prompts_file": the path of a JSON list you wrote under /work. Your own prompts are sent as the user message with the same template and settings; their answers are returned but not graded. "original" runs the unedited weights, "edited" your current edits, and "both" runs both on the same items and returns a paired comparison (the pass-rate difference edited - original over problems with its standard error, and how many samples went from failing to passing and back). The sampling seed of every answer is fixed by its item and sample number, in every pass and for both models (so the two models' answers to a problem largely share their random numbers, though long answers drift apart once a token differs). Every answer to a practice problem is graded by running its extracted code against the problem's tests. You get, per model, the pass rate (overall, by source and by difficulty), the mean length, the share cut at max_tokens, the share flagged as looping (the answer's last 200 characters occur at least 3 times in its last 20,000), and the failure counts by category: cut_at_max_tokens, no_code (no ```python block after </think>), syntax_error, wrong_interface (a function problem whose entry point is not defined), runtime_error (by exception type), timeout, wrong_answer. The answers are in /work/gen_<k>.jsonl (with "both": /work/gen_<k>_original.jsonl and /work/gen_<k>_edited.jsonl), one JSON object per answer with id, sample, text, n_tokens, finish_reason, code (the extracted block), status, exc, loop, source and difficulty. With "activations", for every answer the residual stream at the requested hidden indices (0 = the embeddings, h = 1..24 = the output of the decoder layer whose tensors are named model.language_model.layers.<h-1>.*) is saved, taken at the last token of the prompt and averaged over the answer's first 8,192 tokens, and with "mlp" the same two for the input of those decoder layers' mlp.down_proj: /work/gen_<k>_acts/ (with "both" one folder per model, gen_<k>_acts_original/ and gen_<k>_acts_edited/) holds resid_last.npy and resid_mean.npy (answers x layers x 1,024), mlp_last.npy and mlp_mean.npy (answers x mlp layers x 3,584), as float16, and index.json, which lists each row's id, sample and status.
 (b) TEACHER-FORCED: the model reads up to 1,024 texts of up to 32,768 tokens each, at most 524,288 tokens in total (no generation; it takes seconds to a few minutes). Reply with a ```forward block containing JSON:
 {"type": "teacher_forced", "model": "original" or "edited", "texts": ["raw text", ...] or "chats": [[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}], ...] (add "enable_thinking": true for the thinking template), "return": {"token_logprobs": true, "topk": k (at most 50), "hidden_states": [hidden indices 0..24], "mlp_act": [decoder layers 0..23], "attn_layers": [full-attention layers only (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23); at most 2 texts of at most 2,048 tokens]}}
 "texts_file" or "chats_file" (a JSON list you wrote under /work) can replace a long list. Texts are tokenized without adding special tokens. The results are .npy files in /work/fwd_<k>/, right-padded to the longest text (at most 6 GB per pass): tokens (int32, -1 = padding), token_logprobs (token_logprobs[i, t] = log p(token t | tokens before t); nan at t = 0 and in padding), topk_ids and topk_logprobs (the next-token distribution after position t), hidden_states (texts x indices x length x 1,024), mlp_act (texts x layers x length x 3,584), attn (texts x layers x 8 heads x length x length), activations as float16, and meta.json (lengths, and which indices each file holds). /work/eval_prompt_format.txt gives the exact evaluation prompt, rendered for one practice problem: to score a generated answer with a teacher-forced pass, send prompt + answer as one raw text in "texts" ("chats" renders assistant turns with the chat template, which can drop or reformat their reasoning). A request that fails or is refused does not count against the budget. A generation pass at full size takes up to about an hour when most answers run to the token limit.

HOW TO WORK.
1. Diagnose first. Look at how the model fails on practice problems: cut off at the token limit (often while repeating itself in its thinking or in its code), no code at all, the wrong interface, code that does not parse, code that crashes, or code that runs and gives wrong answers. The generation summary counts these; read some failing texts. Go after the largest category you can explain. If most failures turn out to be ordinary algorithmic mistakes with no single component behind them, say so with evidence instead of forcing an edit.
2. Localize causally. That a component is more active on passing answers is not enough (passing answers come from easier problems and are shorter). Before relying on a component, show that changing it changes the behaviour you predicted, and try several strengths to see a dose-response.
3. Measure with enough power. Pass rate over n generations has a standard error of about 50/sqrt(n) percentage points: about 4.4 points at 128 generations, 2.2 at 512. Measure with as many answers as a pass allows unless you have a specific reason not to. Compare original and edited weights on the SAME problems, and only within one "model": "both" pass: separate passes do not reproduce each other exactly, even for the same request and weights, so never compare across passes and never repeat an identical request with unchanged edits. Problems the original model solves sometimes but not always carry far more signal per generation than problems it always or never solves. Keep an edit only if its gain is clearly larger than its standard error on problems that were not used to choose it. A lower share of cut-off answers or syntax errors does not by itself mean more passing answers: judge edits by pass rate. Dense measurements help too and are cheap: one teacher-forced pass can read up to 1,024 texts (reference solutions, or better, the model's own passing versus failing continuations) and gives a signal on every token. Edits that change a tensor by a fraction of a percent usually have effects too small to see; test strengths large enough to matter and back off if they hurt.
4. Plan your forward passes (see the budget above): for example one diagnostic generation with activations, teacher-forced passes for dense paired measurements, and a final paired generation ("model": "both") on problems you have not used, to confirm.
5. Work efficiently: state the hypothesis of each code block in its first comment line; work through the model in parts; load things once into kernel variables; print compact summaries, never whole arrays (and never raw lists of vocabulary tokens: the vocabulary contains offensive and adult strings and printing them can get the session refused by the provider's content filter; print token ids, code keywords, punctuation or digits instead; outputs are shown in ASCII only, other characters appear as '?'; likewise print short excerpts of generated texts, at most about 300 characters each, not whole transcripts). Keep /work/notes.md up to date (findings with numbers, edits tried and their measured effect, the current best edit; it is shown to you again when the conversation is restarted). Before every forward pass, write to /work/notes.md the exact current edit (tensors, what was changed, strength) and the problem set, so you can rebuild them after a restart. Keep copies of good edits (for example copy /work/edited to /work/best_1/).
6. EXPLAIN EVERY STEP. Before each code or forward block, explain in plain English what you are about to do, why, and what result would change your plan. A block that comes without an explanation is sent back unrun.

RULES. Not allowed: (a) gradient descent or any other training: no backward passes, autograd or optimizers, and no iterative fitting of weights to a loss; (b) running the model other than through the forward-pass tool: do not implement or simulate the network's computation on any input in the kernel (running the model's generated code with run_tests is fine); (c) memorization edits that store particular problems' solutions or test outputs; (d) internet access or search (there is none). Allowed: any analysis of the weights and of forward-pass results, any use of the practice problems and their tests, and any direct edit of the weights that you compute and that is in scope.

HOW THE SESSION RUNS. It continues until all 20 forward passes are used (replying without a block does not end it earlier). Every 40 turns, or sooner when the conversation grows long, the conversation is restarted: you then get this message again, followed by /work/notes.md and the list of your current edits; the kernel keeps its variables. After the last pass you may still run ```python blocks. Then make your final choice (the tensors in /work/edited when you finish are submitted) and reply without a block, saying what you changed (tensors, indices, strength, how many weights), the mechanism you found, the evidence for it (paired differences with their standard errors on problems not used to choose the edit), why you expect it to help on unseen coding problems, and what it might hurt.

THIS RUN.
You do not start from the unedited model. /work/edited already holds the combination of two earlier runs' final edits, both built on a third run's edit (nine tensors in all), and /start holds a read-only copy of the same files and /start/report.md, which explains the combination and contains both runs' final reports. Read the report first. You may keep, change or remove any part of the starting edit, but this run's target is the one below, and another run is changing the starting edit's answer endings at the same time.

THE STARTING EDIT, in short (the report has the details):
- E2, loop exit: five repetition-detector neurons (layer 10 neurons 59 and 120, layer 13 neurons 16 and 7, layer 14 neuron 239) are wired to the model's end-of-thinking direction, at strength 2.5.
- E3, answer end: layer 13 neuron 1420 is wired to an answer-complete direction, so the turn ends after the first solution block closes.
- Neuron 3109, end-of-turn brake: layer 23 MLP neuron 3109 is repurposed to cancel the detectors' push on <|im_end|> where they fire strongly, so prose answers that copy a draft from the thinking are no longer cut short.
- Function-name gates: rank-1 edits of the output gates of attention heads (self_attn.q_proj of layer 19 heads 0, 2, 5, 6, 7, layer 15 head 7 and layer 23 heads 0, 1) make the model copy the given function name after "def".

THE EVALUATION IS BROADER THAN "HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED" SAYS. Besides the code benchmarks, the same protocol and settings are used on four more held-out suites, each with its own user message:
- instruction-following prompts: a writing task with one or more verifiable instructions. The answer after the last </think> is checked by strict automatic checkers; a prompt counts only if every instruction is followed.
- multiple-choice questions (ten options, many subjects), answered with "The answer is (X)" after the reasoning;
- competition math, graded on the last \boxed{} after the last </think>;
- competitive-programming problems (standard input and function form), graded like the code benchmarks.
You never see these suites.

YOUR TARGET: INSTRUCTIONS THAT CONSTRAIN THE WHOLE ANSWER. An evaluation of the starting edit on held-out instruction-following prompts you do not have, with this run's sampling settings, found that it follows about 61% of the prompts fully and 67% of the single instructions. The instruction types followed least, with the approximate share of those instructions followed:
- repeat the request word for word before answering: about 40%;
- a given letter appearing at least, or fewer than, N times: about 35% (this needs counting, and may be out of reach);
- at least or at most N words: about 55%; number of paragraphs: about 50%; number of sentences: about 70%;
- no commas anywhere in the response: about 65%;
- the whole response in lowercase: about 65%;
- words in all capital letters at least, or fewer than, N times: about 50%;
- a keyword at least N times: about 65%; a number of highlighted sections: about 70%.
Two of these got worse when neuron 3109 was added: all lowercase from about 77% to 67%, and the capital-word limits from about 72% to 50%. Its answers are longer, and each extra sentence is another chance to break a rule that applies to the whole answer.

YOUR GOAL is to raise the share of these instructions that the model follows, without lowering the others. Choose the types where you find a clear mechanism; you do not need to cover them all. One kind of mechanism to look for: the prompt states a constraint ("no commas", "all lowercase"), and the answer drifts away from it as it grows. Repairs that act on the specific situation are in scope, for example lowering commas only when the prompt forbids them, or keeping lowercase only when the prompt asks for it. Raising or lowering a token regardless of context is out of scope.

DO NOT CHANGE THE STARTING EDIT'S TENSORS: the mlp tensors of layers 10, 13, 14 and 23, and the q_proj tensors of layers 15, 19 and 23. Another run is working on them, on answers that restart after </think>. Put your edits in other tensors, so that the two runs' edits can be combined afterwards.

HOW TO TEST IT.
- Write your own instruction-following prompts with "prompts" or "prompts_file", in the style above. Write new prompts: do not reproduce prompts of public benchmarks from memory.
- Check the answers in the kernel with your own checkers, on the text after the last </think>.
- Keep separate prompt sets for choosing and for confirming, and make the confirmation sets large enough to see a change of a few points for the types you target.
- Check that the code practice problems do not get worse ("baseline": "start"), and that a few math problems with known answers still end with a correct boxed answer.

COMPARING WITH THE STARTING EDIT. "model": "start" runs the starting edit (always the files in /start, whatever /work/edited holds). In a generation with "model": "both", add "baseline": "start" to run the starting edit and your current edits on the same items and get the paired difference edited - start; without it the baseline is the unedited model, as described above. Teacher-forced passes take "model": "start" too. In the kernel, the starting edit's tensors are /start/<tensor name>.npy.

SETTINGS OF THIS RUN. Every generation uses presence penalty 1.5, and so does the evaluation. This run's GPU is smaller than the other run's: generations of the unedited model, which often loop to the token limit, take several times longer than those of the starting edit, so prefer "baseline": "start". You have 20 forward passes.

YOUR FINAL REPORT, in addition to what HOW THE SESSION RUNS asks, gives the paired difference of your final edit against the starting edit ("baseline": "start") on:
- your confirmation prompts, per instruction type and in all (prompts and instructions followed);
- code practice problems not used to choose the edit;
- your math check.

---
SESSION RESTART (routine restart after 40 turns). This is a new conversation in the same run; the earlier conversation is not shown to you. The kernel kept its variables. Forward passes used: 12 of 20. Code runs used: 227 of 300. Turns so far: 240.

Your notes, /work/notes.md:
<<<
# Notes (IF-constraint run)
## Constraints
- Start = /start (E2,E3, run A neuron L23 3109, run B q_proj gates L15/19/23). /work/edited initially == /start.
- DO NOT touch: mlp tensors of layers 10,13,14,23; q_proj of layers 15,19,23.
- Target: whole-answer constraints in IF prompts (lowercase, no comma, capital-word freq, word/para/sentence counts, repeat request, keyword freq, highlights).
- Budget: 20 forward passes. Used: 0.
## Log

### Pass 1 (planned): generate, model=start, prompts /work/p1_prompts.json (P1 = 512 IF prompts, choice set from pool[:600], meta /work/p1_meta.json), n=1.
- Current edit: none of mine (/work/edited == /start).
- pool = make_tasks(1,1200) (seeded); choice_tasks=pool[:600], confirm_tasks=pool[600:] (reserve for confirmation).

### Pass 1 result (gen, start, P1 512 prompts): prompts all-followed 72.1%, instructions 73.6%. Per type: capital 33%, words 57%, letter 50%,
  highlight 71%, keyword 75%, capword 75%, paragraphs 75%, no_comma 78%, repeat 79%, sentences 84%, lowercase 89%.
  Failures: 108 violations, 21 '</think>' repeat loops in answer, 13 never closed thinking (word-count prompts loop while numbering words).
  no_comma violations: 1-2 commas; ~1/3 copied from a draft in thinking, rest added in answer at conventions (Dear X, / Sincerely, / poem line ends / Therefore,).
  capital (all caps): answers drift back to normal case mid-answer (THE END|...|The End), sign-offs.
  repeat: 3/10 refusals, 5/7 corrupted copies already present in thinking draft (answer copies draft, not prompt).
  capword 'less than N': fails mostly from pronoun 'I'.
### Pass 2 (planned): TF, model=start, texts /work/tf2_texts.json, meta /work/tf2_meta.json (LC 52, NC 61, CAP 22, CTRL 50 from P1 gens; CODE 25 mbpp ref w/ empty think).
  return token_logprobs, topk 20, hidden [12,22,24]. Current edit: none of mine.

### Pass 2 result (TF start, /work/fwd_2, meta /work/tf2_meta.json; groups LC/NC/CAP/CTRL/CODE):
- RMSNorm is ZERO-CENTRED: out = x/rms*(1+w). Final logit change from residual delta d: E_t.((1+wf)*d)/rms(h24).
- NO COMMA: compliant NC answers keep P(comma) ~1e-4 at all positions (CTRL ~0.03); violating NC answers ~0.01-0.035 from the start (no gradual drift).
  Violating commas sampled at p 0.67-0.99 (Dear X|, Therefore|, [City|, poem line ends); best alternative ('\n\n', ' we', ']', '.') ~4-5 nats lower.
- Probe (logreg C=0.05, rms-normed h22, NC vs all, answer positions; /work/probe_nc_h22_w.npy, b in _b.json): first-5-answer-token score NC 4.7, NC_viol 4.2, CTRL -7.4, LC -7.1, CAP -7.0, CODE -14.
  Thinking last 200: NC -1.8 vs CTRL -5.5. => instruction feature present even in violating answers; the push on commas is too weak vs strong conventions.
- LOWERCASE: only 3/52 LC answers violate (my prompts too easy). P(upper) LC compliant ~1e-3 vs CTRL 0.09-0.16. Violation: one unlucky ' You' (p .05) then self-reinforcing (.36,.77,.88).
- ALL CAPS: 13/22 violate. Before first slip P(lower) ~0.00-0.01; first lowercase token sampled at p .06-.35 (or forced: 'S'+'incerely'); AFTER the slip P(lower) jumps to 0.3-0.76 => collapse/drift.
- Output directions (closed-form weighted ridge on embedding E, weights 1+sqrt(freq in gen_1)): /work/v_up.npy (upper tokens -1, others 0 sd .08),
  /work/v_lo.npy (lowercase-containing -1), /work/v_cm.npy (comma tokens -1, '.'/newline 0). logit change = E_t . v ; residual write d = rms(h)*v/(1+wf).
### PLAN: gated neurons in layer-22 MLP (allowed; NOT 23): gate = constraint-instruction probe (survives slips), up = const dir, down = rms*v/(1+wf) * strength.
  Next: check probe survives the all-caps slip; build probes for LC and CAP; find low-use L22 neurons to repurpose; check orthogonality to L23 neuron 3109 rows.

### Session 2 findings (before pass 3)
- Probes: switched to CLOSED-FORM ridge probes (ridge_probe2, lam_eff=0.1 x trace/1024) on rms-normed h22 to avoid iterative fitting; logistic clf_* only used for diagnosis.
  NC ridge probe: NC answer p5/p50 0.45/0.89; violating-comma predicting positions p5/p50 0.44/0.75; CODE max ~0.1; other-IF-answer p99 0.72 (false positives are LC/CAP answers, harmless).
  Leave-one-template-out: held-out phrasing p50 drops to -0.2..0.8 -> need more phrasing diversity -> pass 3/4.
- Output dirs (weighted ridge, penalty in residual metric ||z/(1+wf)||, protected tokens </think>,<think>,im_end,newlines,'.' pinned 0):
  /work/r_cm.npy = residual dir per nat on ',' (|r| 0.73/nat; 10 nats -> 0.22 of ||h24||; spill: quote-closers/';' -1.3..-2.3 at 10 nats).
  /work/r_lc.npy = coding upper -1 / lower-only +0.2 (lam 3e3), per nat of median twin gap (|r| 2.56/nat; 3 nats: ' You' -2.7 vs ' you' +0.5).
  Residual write for S nats: d = rho*S*r, rho = rms(h24) at answers ~0.36.
- Gate design (layer 22 MLP, pair of neurons = soft step): gate1 = k*(w.x^ + b - s0) [bias via mhat22 direction, mhat.x^ ~ 20+-3],
  gate2 = gate1 - dA, up = mhat/(mu*(1+wln)), down1 = rho*S*r/dA, down2 = -down1. Low-down-norm candidates L22: 1105, 11, 164, 262, 75, 3.
- CAP (all caps) deferred: slips mid-word, case-axis directions weak for it, not in held-out worst list.
### Pass 3 (planned): GENERATE model=start n=1, max_tokens 20000: prompts /work/p3_prompts.json (440 IF choice-phrasings [banks.json choice half],
  24 math, 16 MC; meta /work/p3_meta.json) + problems /work/p3_mbpp_ids.json (32 MBPP). Purpose: baseline on harder prompts + texts for probe training (pass 4 TF).
  Current edit: none of mine (/work/edited == /start).

### Pass 3 result (gen, start, /work/gen_3.jsonl; ids 'prompt/<k>' 0-based -> /work/p3_prompts.json, /work/p3_meta.json; MBPP ids /work/p3_mbpp_ids.json)
- IF (440, choice-bank phrasings in /work/banks.json [choice=first list, confirm=second list; NEVER use confirm wordings before final]):
  per-instruction followed: capital 56% (48), words 58%, letter 63%, highlight 74%, keyword 74%, paragraphs 75%, no_comma 75% (133), capword 79%,
  lowercase 79% (126), sentences 83%, repeat 84%. Prompt-level 71.4%. cut 6.8%, loop 14.5%, no answer 2%.
- math 22/24 boxed correct, MC 15/16, MBPP 9/32 (start).
- Failure anatomy: NC 33 fails: 6 no answer, 10 loop; of those with answers 22/27 have only 1-2 commas (Dear X, | Sincerely, | Best regards, | dates
  'October 26, 2023' | 56% of first violating commas COPIED from the thinking draft) -> need ~10 nats at violation points.
  LC 26 fails: 9 loop, 7 cut; slips = sentence-initial capitals ('It helps', 'They ...', 'Dear aisha'), 22% copied; after a slip drifts to normal case.
  CAP 21 fails: mostly majority-lowercase collapse (frac lower ~0.63).
- Kernel vars: G3 (gen_3 rows), p3_meta, p3_prompts, res3/d3 (grades), items4/d4 (rendered TF texts: render(user)+text, with token counts),
  r_cm, r_lc (output dirs per nat), mhat (const dir), wln22, W_g22/W_u22/W_d22 (orig L22 mlp), FX/lab_* (pass-2 positions, h22 rms-normed), ridge_probe2.
### Pass 4 (planned): TF model=start on /work/tf4_texts.json (meta /work/tf4_meta.json): ~150 pass-3 texts <=3800 tokens:
  NC~55 (all 8 choice wordings), LC~45, CAP~12, OTH~14, mc~12, code~12, math~4. return token_logprobs, topk 20, hidden_states [22], mlp_act [22].
  Purpose: (1) probes with diverse phrasings (combine with pass-2 FX), (2) layer-22 neuron usage to pick neurons to repurpose, (3) P(comma)/P(upper) baselines.

HOW TO WORK.
1. Diagnose first. Look at how the model fails on practice problems: cut off at the token limit (often while repeating itself in its thinking or in its code), no code at all, the wrong interface, code that does not parse, code that crashes, or code that runs and gives wrong answers. The generation summary counts these; read some failing texts. Go after the largest category you can explain. If most failures turn out to be ordinary algorithmic mistakes with no single component behind them, say so with evidence instead of forcing an edit.
2. Localize causally. That a component is more active on passing answers is not enough (passing answers come from easier problems and are shorter). Before relying on a component, show that changing it changes the behaviour you predicted, and try several strengths to see a dose-response.
3. Measure with enough power. Pass rate over n generations has a standard error of about 50/sqrt(n) percentage points: about 4.4 points at 128 generations, 2.2 at 512. Measure with as many answers as a pass allows unless you have a specific reason not to. Compare original and edited weights on the SAME problems, and only within one "model": "both" pass: separate passes do not reproduce each other exactly, even for the same request and weights, so never compare across passes and never repeat an identical request with unchanged edits. Problems the original model solves sometimes but not always carry far more signal per generation than problems it always or never solves. Keep an edit only if its gain is clearly larger than its standard error on problems that were not used to choose it. A lower share of cut-off answers or syntax errors does not by itself mean more passing answers: judge edits by pass rate. Dense measurements help too and are cheap: one teacher-forced pass can read up to 1,024 texts (reference solutions, or better, the model's own passing versus failing continuations) and gives a signal on every token. Edits that change a tensor by a fraction of a percent usually have effects too small to see; test strengths large enough to matter and back off if they hurt.
4. Plan your forward passes (see the budget above): for example one diagnostic generation with activations, teacher-forced passes for dense paired measurements, and a final paired generation ("model": "both") on problems you have not used, to confirm.
5. Your job is to make it better at writing correct programs by EDITING ITS WEIGHTS DIRECTLY: find out what goes wrong inside the network when it fails at programming problems and repair that with targeted changes.

HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED. After you finish, your edited model and the unedited model are evaluated on held-out code-generation benchmarks (Python functions specified by a description with an example test, or by a signature and docstring) with this fixed protocol: the chat template with thinking enabled (enable_thinking=True: the model reasons between <think> and </think>, then answers); the user message is the problem statement, a blank line and "Write a complete, self-contained Python 3 solution. Put your final code in a single ```python block at the end of your answer."; sampling with temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0 and presence penalty 1.5, and at most 32,768 new tokens for reasoning and answer together. The last ```python block after </think> is extracted; only its imports, definitions and top-level assignments are kept (example calls and asserts the model adds are dropped), and it is run in a sandbox against the problem's hidden unit tests, with a time limit. A sample is correct only if every test passes. The config, tokenizer, chat template and decoding settings are fixed: only weight values can change (same tensor names and shapes; your edits are cast to bfloat16, the model's dtype). You never see these benchmarks.

WHAT COUNTS. We want edits that come from understanding the network: find out what goes wrong when it fails at programming problems, identify the components responsible (specific neurons, heads, directions or circuits) and change them in a way you can justify with evidence. Repairing a specific failure mechanism is in scope. For example, if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, because it never closes or never opens its code block, because it drifts into another language or into prose, because it renames the function it was asked for, or because a systematic pattern makes its code fail to parse, then finding and fixing what drives that counts. Out of scope, and refused by save_edit: the final norm (model.language_model.norm.weight), the input embedding / output layer (model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight, which is tied to the output layer), and any edit that only multiplies a whole tensor by a constant. Also out of scope: global knobs (making the whole output distribution sharper or flatter; raising or lowering particular tokens, such as code fences or end-of-turn, regardless of context); making the model skip its thinking or close it early regardless of the problem; and writing particular problems' solutions or test outputs into the weights (memorization edits). The discordant list points somewhere specific. Of the 21 pairs where only start followed the keyword instruction, 10 come from prompts that also ban commas, 4 from lowercase prompts and 5 from plain ones. Answers are not shorter overall: median 72 versus 74 words.

My hypothesis is that the loss sits where the comma ban and a keyword count meet. The model drafts and checks the keyword count in its thinking and then copies the draft. My comma push forces it off the draft at each comma, and the rewritten answer drops keyword uses.

To test this, I will split the keyword pairs by whether the prompt also bans commas or asks for lowercase. I will also measure how much of each answer is copied verbatim from its thinking: the share of the answer's 8-word shingles that appear in the thinking. The hypothesis predicts a lower copy share for edited answers to comma-ban prompts.

```python
# Hypothesis: keyword loss concentrates in NC+keyword prompts, where comma suppression lowers verbatim copying of the (keyword-checked) thinking draft.
def think_of(t): return t.rsplit('</think>',1)[0] if '</think>' in t else t
def copy_share(t, n=8):
    a=ans_of(t).split(); th=set()
    tw=think_of(t).split()
    th={' '.join(tw[j:j+n]) for j in range(len(tw)-n+1)}
    sh=[' '.join(a[j:j+n]) for j in range(len(a)-n+1)]
    return np.mean([s in th for s in sh]) if sh else np.nan
def grp(o): return 'NC' if 'no_comma' in o else ('LC' if 'lowercase' in o else ('plain' if not o else 'other'))
K['g']=K.others.apply(grp)
for g,sub in K.groupby('g'):

GG={'C1':(G9s,G9e),'C2':(G10s,G10e),'C3':(G12s,G12e)}

K['ecopy']=[copy_share(GG[r.set][1][f'prompt/{r.i}']['text']) for r in K.itertuples()]
```

There is a cheap and exact way to see whether my gate is even active on keyword answers. My edit changes nothing upstream of layer 22's MLP, so the gate's input on any text is identical under start and v3. I already have that input (`XX`, rms-normed x_mid22 at sampled positions of the pass-4 and pass-7 texts, which include some keyword prompts). I will compare thinking and answer positions of keyword texts against comma-ban texts.
- If f is near zero on keyword answers and thinking, v3 cannot act on them, and the dip is resampling noise.

The plain keyword prompts lose 6 pairs and gain 1 under the substring checker (p≈0.13). There, the gate fires at 17% on average, so cross-firing is a candidate cause, though a weak one. Most of the keyword drop is in comma-ban combos, where the gate must fire, and those break even at prompt level.

A tighter gate cuts cross-firing roughly in half. At t0 0.05, t1 0.45, mean firing drops on keyword answers from 0.17 to 0.07, on other prompts from 0.26 to 0.17 and on all-caps from 0.42 to 0.29. Comma-ban answers drop from 0.85 to 0.79.

The mean over all positions of comma-ban answers is the wrong measure of what I would lose. What matters is the push at the positions where a comma is likely. The pass-4 teacher-forced data (start model) has, for the comma-ban answers, the exact layer-22 MLP input and the start model's next-token distribution. So I can compute the gate's firing at comma-risk positions (start P(comma) > 2%) and at positions where start actually emitted a violating comma. I will do this for each candidate threshold. I will also check firing over the first answer tokens, where greeting commas ("Dear Customer,") still escape under v3.

If tightening keeps nearly full push at comma-risk positions, I will build v4 with tighter thresholds. If it loses much push there, I keep v3's thresholds.

```python

fd='/work/fwd_4'; meta4=json.load(open(fd+'/meta.json'))
toks=np.load(fd+'/tokens.npy'); tki=np.load(fd+'/topk_ids.npy',mmap_mode='r'); tkl=np.load(fd+'/topk_logprobs.npy',mmap_mode='r')
hs=np.load(fd+'/hidden_states.npy',mmap_mode='r'); ma=np.load(fd+'/mlp_act.npy',mmap_mode='r')
print({k:v for k,v in meta4.items() if k!='lengths'}, hs.shape, ma.shape)
CM=tok.convert_tokens_to_ids(','); ET=tok.convert_tokens_to_ids('</think>'); print('comma id',CM,'</think> id',ET)
Wd=W_d22.numpy() if hasattr(W_d22,'numpy') else W_d22
rows_=[]
for i,e in enumerate(m4):
    if e['cat']!='NC': continue
    tt=toks[i]; L=int((tt>=0).sum()); pe=np.where(tt[:L]==ET)[0]
    if len(pe)==0: continue
    a0_=pe[-1]+1
    pos=np.arange(a0_,L-1)
    ids=tki[i,pos]; lps=tkl[i,pos].astype(np.float32)
    pcm=np.where(ids==CM, np.exp(lps), 0).sum(1)

def fof(s,a0,a1): kk=dA_/(a1-a0); gg=kk*(s-a0); return (silu(gg)-silu(gg-dA_))/dA_
for (a0,a1) in [(-0.15,0.35),(0.0,0.4),(0.05,0.45),(0.1,0.5)]:

print('score quantiles at risk pos:', np.quantile(R[R.pcm>.02].s,[.05,.1,.25,.5]).round(2), ' at emitted:', np.quantile(R[R.emit].s,[.05,.1,.25,.5]).round(2) if R.emit.sum() else None)
```

Under the current thresholds (t0 −0.15, t1 0.35) the gate is well placed on comma-ban answers:

| | mean f | share with f < 0.5 |
|---|---|---|
| comma-risk positions (start P(comma) > 2%) | 0.95 | 1.5% |
| positions where start emitted a comma | 0.95 | 0% |
| first five answer tokens | 0.97 | — |

So the greeting commas that survive ("Dear Customer,") are not under-gated. Their prior is simply above 10 nats.

Tightening to t0 0.05, t1 0.45 would leave 14% of the emitted-comma positions with less than half the push. And these comma-ban texts were in the probe's training set, so on held-out wordings the scores, and the coverage, will be lower. The decision therefore needs held-out data:
- how much push tightening would remove at comma-risk positions in held-out comma-ban answers;
- how strongly the gate cross-fires on held-out answers to other prompt types.

The C1–C3 start-arm generations are ideal for this. They use held-out wordings and tasks, and under v3 the gate's input on them equals start's.

A teacher-forced pass returning h23 and the layer-22 MLP activations costs about 9.2 KB per token across the padded length, so I must keep texts short. 27 of 32 failures are corrupted copies. They regularize word forms ("skim"→"skimming", "confident"→"confidence") or garble into rare pieces ("sorduhub", "alreadysomethi"). v3 changes the distribution essentially only at commas. Keyword tokens are untouched, and so are answer and thinking tokens in general. The keyword dip in generation must come from thinking trajectories that diverge by sampling, not from a pathway in the edit.

There is one surprise. At held-out comma-risk positions, P(comma) drops only from a median 0.62 to 0.019, about 4.4 nats of log-odds, although the design pushes 10 nats at full firing. Two explanations are possible:

I will regress the measured log-odds change on the gate firing f at each comma-risk position, using pass 13's x_mid22. If the change at f≈1 is near −10, the gate's coverage is what limits the effect.
